title: Root subgroups and coroots of a reductive group
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], smoothness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme], and finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $\mathbf G_a$ and $\mathbf G_m$ for the additive and multiplicative group schemes [def-sc-gm-ga]. A torus is a group scheme becoming $\mathbf G_m^r$ over an algebraic closure; split means already isomorphic to this product over $F$, and maximal means maximal under inclusion. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type which is reductive, meaning that it has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup scheme. Here unipotent means that every geometric point is a unipotent matrix in a faithful linear representation. Let $T\subseteq G$ be a split maximal torus. Let $\mathfrak g$ be the tangent space of $G$ at the identity, with the action of $T$ obtained by differentiating conjugation on $G$. Let $\Phi$ be the nontrivial characters $\alpha:T\to\mathbf G_m$ occurring as weights in this action: $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ is the subspace on which $t$ acts by $\alpha(t)$. We use characters of $T$, not their differentials. For every $\alpha\in\Phi$ there is a unique smooth connected closed subgroup $U_\alpha\subseteq G$ normalized by $T$ whose tangent space is $\mathfrak g_\alpha$. It is isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$. For any group-scheme isomorphism $u_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\alpha$ one has
$$t\,u_\alpha(a)\,t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)\qquad(t\in T(A),\ a\in A)$$
for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. There is a group-scheme homomorphism $\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_m\to T$ satisfying
$$\alpha(\alpha^\vee(s))=s^2\qquad(s\in A^\times)$$
for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(b),(c),(e), printed pp.428--430, and 21.19, printed p.431 (formula (135))

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\Phi$. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] to $(G,T)$: its reductivity and maximal-torus hypotheses are exactly those here. It gives $\dim_F\mathfrak g_\alpha=1$ and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. Consequently the sum of the adjoint weight spaces on the positive rational ray through $\alpha$ is exactly $\mathfrak g_\alpha$.

Apply [lem-sfb-torus-positive-ray-subgroup] to the conjugation action of $S=T$ on $H=G$, with $\eta=\alpha$. It constructs a smooth connected unipotent closed $T$-stable subgroup $U_\alpha$ with tangent space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$. If $K$ is another smooth connected closed $T$-stable subgroup with that tangent space, both implications of that lemma give $U_\alpha\subseteq K\subseteq U_\alpha$, hence equality as subgroup schemes. Its tangent space has dimension one by step 1, so [lem-sfb-one-dimensional-unipotent-additive] gives the required group-scheme isomorphism with $\mathbf G_a$.

Fix any group-scheme isomorphism $u:\mathbf G_a\to U_\alpha$. Transport conjugation through $u$. Write $R=F[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_r^{\pm1}]=F[T]$ using a splitting of $T$ and [def-sc-gm-ga]. At the universal point of $T$ this action is an $R$-automorphism of $\mathbf A^1_R$ fixing zero, hence a polynomial $P(X)$ with polynomial inverse $Q(X)$. Since $R$ is a domain, $\deg(P\circ Q)=\deg P\deg Q=1$; thus $P(X)=cX$ with $c\in R^\times$. On the tangent line its multiplier is $c$. But $du$ identifies that line with $\mathfrak g_\alpha$, so the definition of the $T$-weight gives $c=\alpha\in F[T]^\times$. This polynomial identity over $F[T]$ specializes along every $F[T]\to A$, giving $t u(a)t^{-1}=u(\alpha(t)a)$ for all commutative $F$-algebras $A$, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Paragraphs 14.59--14.60, printed p.298, and 21.19, printed p.431, formula (135); universal Laurent-polynomial calculation written out.

proof.text:
The cocharacter $\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_m	o T$ supplied by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] has $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\veeangle=2$. The pairing in its statement is defined by $\chi\circ
u(s)=s^{\langle\chi,
uangle}$, so substituting $\chi=\alpha$ and $
u=\alpha^\vee$ gives $\alpha(\alpha^\vee(s))=s^2$ on every test algebra. If $\Phi$ is empty all assertions indexed by $\alpha$ are vacuous.
